title: the father runs
hook: the father runs — old men didn't run

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Good Samaritan. The man from across the line who stopped. Your line was: the neighbor is whoever is in front of you. Who was in front of you? Day eleven.

A grown son is walking up a dusty road toward the house he grew up in. He hasn't been home in a long time. He left badly. He said things. He took money that wasn't really his yet, and it's gone. Now he's broke, and he's practicing a speech in his head, the way you might rehearse a hard phone call. He's not hoping to be forgiven. He's hoping to be hired. And then, while he's still far off, before he's close enough to say a word, he sees his father, an old man, running toward him. Today's story is that run.
screen: `A SON WHO LEFT BADLY.` → `A SPEECH, REHEARSED.` → `AN OLD MAN, RUNNING.`

segments.voice: It's in Luke's Gospel, chapter fifteen, and it's usually called the Prodigal Son. Prodigal isn't in the story. It's an old word for wasteful, and the name was given later. A man has two sons. The younger one asks for his share of the inheritance now, while his father's still alive. Some readers hear in that: I wish you were already gone. The father gives it to him. The son goes off to a far country and spends every coin. Then a famine hits, and he ends up feeding pigs, hungry enough to envy what they eat. And then the King James Bible says: "when he came to himself." He rehearses his speech. I've sinned. I'm not worthy to be your son. Make me one of your hired workers. Now here's the moment. "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." Some scholars of the period point out that a dignified older man didn't run in public. The text only says he ran, and doesn't stop to explain. Had compassion is the same Greek word Luke uses for the Samaritan in yesterday's story. It means his gut turned over. The son starts the speech, and the father never lets him get to the part about being a servant. He calls for the best robe, a ring, shoes, and a feast. "For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found." But the story isn't over. The older brother, who stayed and worked, hears the party and won't go in. And the father goes out to him too, and pleads with him. The story ends there. We never find out if he goes in. Christians have long heard it as a picture of God: a father who runs to the one who left, and walks out to the one who stayed.
screen: `HIS SHARE, NOW.` · `FEEDING PIGS, FAR FROM HOME.` · `THE FATHER RUNS.` · `THE OLDER BROTHER, OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `HE WAS LOST, AND IS FOUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let a breath out. Think of a place, or a person, you've drifted from. Maybe you left badly. Maybe it just faded. Picture the road back. Now picture them seeing you from far off, and coming toward you before you've said anything. Stay with that picture. If you pray, you can hold the father's words, he was lost, and is found. If you don't, just let the picture be. Forty-five seconds. The bell holds the time.
The Prodigal Son. The one who wasted everything, and the father who ran to meet him anyway. Eleventh word.
Your line: you can come home. Today, send one message to someone you've drifted from. It doesn't have to be a speech. Hello is enough. Day eleven.

screen: `DAY 11 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "BLESSED ARE THE POOR IN SPIRIT".`

howItsDone: Christians read the Prodigal Son as a picture of God's welcome to anyone who returns. The Orthodox calendar names a Sunday before Lent after it, and Catholic and Orthodox teaching often connects it with confession and repentance.

match.prompt: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
pairs: asked for his share, and spent it
ran, and fell on his neck
heard the party and wouldn't go in

myth: the word prodigal appears in the story itself
it doesn't. prodigal means wasteful, and the name was given to the story later.
the story ends with the older brother joining the feast
it ends with the father pleading with him outside. we never find out if he goes in.
the father's "had compassion" is the same Greek word Luke uses for the Samaritan
it means his gut turned over. Luke uses it in both stories.

fork.setup: you're the father. your younger son, who took his inheritance and wasted it, appears far down the road. he hasn't said a word yet. what do you do?
options: wait at the door to hear his apology.
run to him, and throw your arms around him.
send a servant to find out what he wants.
fork.reveal: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran." a dignified old man running in public, before a word of the speech.

original.note: Greek. he had compassion; literally, his gut was moved. Luke uses it for the Samaritan (10:33) and for the running father (15:20).

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a bad son who learned his lesson.
what it means: a story about a father who runs to the one who left and walks out to the one who stayed.
what a scholar hears: it ends open. the older brother is still outside, and Luke never says whether he goes in. Luke 15 tells it right after the lost sheep and the lost coin.

sources.quoted: But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.

notes: 'A dignified older man didn't run in public' is attributed to 'people who study the period' (a common reading, e.g. Kenneth Bailey); the text itself says only that he ran. Confirm framing.
Asking for the inheritance early described as 'close to saying, I wish you were already gone', a widely held reading, not stated in the text. Confirm.
ἐσπλαγχνίσθη (splanchnizomai, aorist) used in Luke 10:33 and 15:20; pronunciation given in reconstructed style. Confirm.
